THOUGHT: The patient is a young (32-year-old) man with a 2-month history of progressive fatigue and severe pruritus, scleral icterus, and numerous scratch marks — all consistent with cholestatic liver disease. Laboratory testing shows a primarily cholestatic pattern (markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase 460 U/L with only mild transaminase elevation and mild hyperbilirubinemia). He has a 5-year history of ulcerative colitis, which has a strong association with primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC), classically affecting younger men. Imaging notes thickening of the bile ducts and focal bile duct dilatation, consistent with the “beading”/irregularity of the intra- and extrahepatic ducts seen in PSC. Antimitochondrial antibody is negative, making primary biliary cholangitis (which typically affects middle-aged women and is AMA-positive) much less likely. Other causes (acute viral hepatitis, choledocholithiasis, obstructing mass) are less consistent with the pattern of findings, demographics, and the imaging description. Therefore the constellation of cholestatic LFTs, pruritus, characteristic biliary imaging changes, and underlying ulcerative colitis points to primary sclerosing cholangitis as the most likely diagnosis.

DIAGNOSIS: Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC)
